claim: Flagellar-driven motility grants unicellular organisms the ability to gather more food and avoid predators.
source: Flagellar-driven motility grants unicellular organisms the ability to gather more food and avoid predators, but the energetic costs of construction and operation of flagella are considerable.
evidence: This is a general statement about flagellar function that draws from established biological understanding.

claim: The energetic costs of construction and operation of flagella are considerable.
source: Flagellar-driven motility grants unicellular organisms the ability to gather more food and avoid predators, but the energetic costs of construction and operation of flagella are considerable.
evidence: This is supported by the detailed cost calculations presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Only cells with larger cell volumes than the typical bacterium could evolve the more expensive eukaryotic flagellum.
source: However, a comparison of whole-cell costs and flagellum costs across the Tree of Life reveals that only cells with larger cell volumes than the typical bacterium could evolve the more expensive eukaryotic flagellum.
evidence: This is supported by the comparative cost analysis shown in Figure 4 and the calculations presented in the manuscript.

claim: The cost-effectiveness of bacterial and eukaryotic flagella follows a common trend.
source: The benefits of flagellar investment were analysed in terms of swimming speed, nutrient collection, and growth rate; showing, among other things, that the cost-effectiveness of bacterial and eukaryotic flagella follows a common trend.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data in Figure 2C showing swimming speed per ATP invested.

claim: The three domains of life each carry their own type of flagellum.
source: These findings provide insight into the unsolved evolutionary question of why the three domains of life each carry their own type of flagellum.
evidence: This is established biological knowledge about the diversity of flagellar types.

claim: The bacterial flagellum consists of a helical protein filament that is attached via a hook region to a basal body embedded in the cell envelope.
source: The bacterial flagellum (Berg, 2003) consists of a helical protein filament, sometimes sheathed by a membrane (Geis et al., 1993), that is attached, via a hook region, to a basal body embedded in the cell envelope.
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature on bacterial flagellar structure.

claim: The bacterial flagellum filament is assembled by progressive addition of monomers of the protein flagellin (FliC) to the tip.
source: The filament is assembled by progressive addition of monomers of the protein flagellin (FliC) to the tip, reached by diffusion through a central channel in the filament.
evidence: This describes the established mechanism of bacterial flagellar assembly.

claim: Bacterial flagellum rotation is driven by a proton or sodium gradient.
source: Its rotation is driven by a proton or sodium gradient (Ito and Takahashi, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to literature on bacterial flagellar motors.

claim: The archaeal flagellum filament lacks a central channel and is assembled from the base.
source: The filament, lacking a central channel, is assembled from the base, and its rotation is driven by ATP hydrolysis (Albers and Jarrell, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to literature on archaeal flagellar structure and assembly.

claim: Archaeal flagellum rotation is driven by ATP hydrolysis.
source: The filament, lacking a central channel, is assembled from the base, and its rotation is driven by ATP hydrolysis (Albers and Jarrell, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to literature on archaeal flagellar motors.

claim: The eukaryotic flagellum diameter is an order of magnitude larger than bacterial and archaeal flagella.
source: Its diameter is an order of magnitude larger (Khan and Scholey, 2018); it bends rather than rotates; and the ATP-dependent bending is caused by motor proteins arranged along the length of the flagellum.
evidence: This is supported by citation to literature on eukaryotic flagellar structure.

claim: The eukaryotic flagellum bends rather than rotates.
source: Its diameter is an order of magnitude larger (Khan and Scholey, 2018); it bends rather than rotates; and the ATP-dependent bending is caused by motor proteins arranged along the length of the flagellum.
evidence: This is established knowledge about eukaryotic flagellar mechanics.

claim: The ATP-dependent bending of eukaryotic flagella is caused by motor proteins arranged along the length of the flagellum.
source: Its diameter is an order of magnitude larger (Khan and Scholey, 2018); it bends rather than rotates; and the ATP-dependent bending is caused by motor proteins arranged along the length of the flagellum.
evidence: This is established knowledge about eukaryotic flagellar mechanics.

claim: Most eukaryotic flagella have two single microtubules in the middle, surrounded by nine doublet microtubules.
source: Most eukaryotic flagella have two single microtubules in the middle, surrounded by nine doublet microtubules.
evidence: This describes the canonical 9+2 structure of eukaryotic flagella, which is established knowledge.

claim: The eukaryotic axoneme is always surrounded by a membrane.
source: This whole protein complex, the axoneme, is always surrounded by a membrane.
evidence: This is established knowledge about eukaryotic flagellar structure.

claim: The eukaryotic axoneme is assembled at the tip with subunit delivery facilitated by active intraflagellar transport (IFT).
source: Like the bacterial flagellum, the eukaryotic axoneme is assembled at the tip, but with subunit delivery being facilitated by active intraflagellar transport (IFT) (Marshall and Rosenbaum, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to literature on eukaryotic flagellar assembly.

claim: For E. coli, the construction and operating costs of flagella are 2% and 0.1%, respectively, relative to total cell energy expenditure.
source: For E. coli, the construction and operating costs are 2% and 0.1%, respectively, relative to total cell energy expenditure (Macnab, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work on E. coli flagellar costs.

claim: The operating cost of E. coli flagella is 3.4% assuming 5 flagella, a 100 Hz rotation rate, and a 1 hr cell division time.
source: Others found an operating cost of 3.4% (assuming 5 flagella, a 100 Hz rotation rate, and a 1 hr cell division time) (Ziegler and Takors, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to another study on E. coli flagellar costs.

claim: The relative construction cost for the dinoflagellate flagellum was estimated at 0.026%.
source: The relative construction cost for the dinoflagellate was estimated at 0.026%.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work on dinoflagellate flagellar costs.

claim: The relative operating cost of dinoflagellate flagella was 0.08–0.9%, compared to total cell maintenance cost.
source: The relative operating cost was 0.08–0.9%, compared to total cell maintenance cost (Lynch and Marinov, 2015; Raven and Richardson, 1984).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on dinoflagellate flagellar costs.

claim: The average volume per amino acid is 1.33 × 10^-10 µm^3.
source: When only the volume of a protein is known, we calculate the number of amino acids using the average volume per amino acid (1.33 × 10–10 µm3; Methods).
evidence: This is a calculated value based on established physical properties of amino acids.

claim: The construction cost per µm of E. coli flagellum is 3.02 × 10^7 ATP.
source: Construction cost per µm (ATP)	3.02 × 107
evidence: This is a calculated value presented in Table 1.

claim: The construction cost per E. coli flagellum is 2.32 × 10^8 ATP.
source: Construction cost per flagellum (ATP)	2.32 × 108
evidence: This is a calculated value presented in Table 1.

claim: E. coli has an average of 3.4 flagella per cell.
source: Number of flagella per cell	3.4
evidence: This is data from literature cited in the manuscript (Harshey and Matsuyama, 1994; Turner et al., 2000).

claim: The construction cost of all E. coli flagella is 7.88 × 10^8 ATP cell^-1.
source: Construction cost of all flagella (ATP cell–1)	7.88 × 108
evidence: This is a calculated value presented in Table 1.

claim: E. coli has a cell volume of 1.0 µm^3.
source: Cell volume (µm3)	1.0
evidence: This is a standard value for E. coli cell volume.

claim: E. coli has a cell division time of 1.0 hr.
source: Cell division time (hr)	1.0
evidence: This is a standard value for E. coli under optimal growth conditions.

claim: The total cost of E. coli cell (construction + operating) is 1.59 × 10^10 ATP.
source: Total cost of cell (construction + operating; ATP)	1.59 × 1010
evidence: This is a calculated value presented in Table 1, based on cited previous work (Lynch and Marinov, 2015).

claim: The relative construction cost of all E. coli flagella is 5.0%.
source: Relative construction cost, all flagella (%)	5.0
evidence: This is a calculated value presented in Table 1.

claim: The operating cost per E. coli flagellum is 6.6 × 10^4 ATP s^-1.
source: Operating cost per flagellum (ATP s–1)	6.6 × 104
evidence: This is a calculated value presented in Table 1.

claim: The operating cost per E. coli cell cycle for all flagella is 8.08 × 10^8 ATP.
source: Operating cost per cell cycle, all flagella (ATP)	8.08 × 108
evidence: This is a calculated value presented in Table 1.

claim: The relative operating cost of all E. coli flagella is 5.2%.
source: Relative operating cost, all flagella (%)	5.2
evidence: This is a calculated value presented in Table 1.

claim: The relative total cost of all E. coli flagella is 10.2%.
source: Relative total cost, all flagella (%)	10.2
evidence: This is a calculated value presented in Table 1.

claim: A large fraction (0.99) of the E. coli flagellum cost is in the filament (including the hook).
source: A large fraction of this cost, 0.99, is in the filament (including the hook).
evidence: This is a calculated value from the detailed cost breakdown.

claim: The E. coli flagellum is 7.5 µm long.
source: Using protein lengths and copy numbers, we calculated the energy costs for each protein per flagellum, and by summing these, obtained the cost for the whole flagellum. The total cost of a single 7.5 µm long (Turner et al., 2000) flagellum is 2.32 × 108 ATP.
evidence: This is data from cited literature (Turner et al., 2000).

claim: The maximum number of stators per E. coli flagellum is at least 11.
source: The maximum number of stators, per flagellum, is at least 11 (Reid et al., 2006), each of which has two channels (Braun and Blair, 2001), and each channel passes 50 protons per revolution (Gabel and Berg, 2003; Samuel and Berg, 1996), leading to an estimated 1100 protons per revolution, which is similar to the value determined experimentally for Streptococcus, 1240 protons per revolution (Meister et al., 1987).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on bacterial flagellar motors.

claim: Each E. coli flagellar stator has two channels.
source: The maximum number of stators, per flagellum, is at least 11 (Reid et al., 2006), each of which has two channels (Braun and Blair, 2001), and each channel passes 50 protons per revolution (Gabel and Berg, 2003; Samuel and Berg, 1996), leading to an estimated 1100 protons per revolution, which is similar to the value determined experimentally for Streptococcus, 1240 protons per revolution (Meister et al., 1987).
evidence: This is supported by citation to literature on bacterial flagellar motors.

claim: Each channel in the E. coli flagellar stator passes 50 protons per revolution.
source: The maximum number of stators, per flagellum, is at least 11 (Reid et al., 2006), each of which has two channels (Braun and Blair, 2001), and each channel passes 50 protons per revolution (Gabel and Berg, 2003; Samuel and Berg, 1996), leading to an estimated 1100 protons per revolution, which is similar to the value determined experimentally for Streptococcus, 1240 protons per revolution (Meister et al., 1987).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on bacterial flagellar motors.

claim: The E. coli flagellum can spin at a maximal rate of 380 Hz.
source: The E. coli flagellum can spin at a maximal rate of 380 Hz (Chen and Berg, 2000; Gabel and Berg, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on bacterial flagellar rotation rates.

claim: The mean swimming speed for Salmonella occurs at a rotation rate of 150 Hz.
source: The mean swimming speed for Salmonella, a close relative of E. coli, occurs at a rotation rate of 150 Hz (Magariyama et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to literature on Salmonella flagellar rotation.

claim: The proton/ATP ratio in the ATP synthase is 3.33.
source: The energetic costs of this can be expressed in terms of the number of ATP hydrolyses by using the proton/ATP ratio in the ATP synthase, which is 3.33 (Jiang et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to literature on ATP synthase.

claim: The major filament component in Pyrococcus furiosus is FlaB0.
source: The major filament component in P. furiosus is FlaB0 (Nather et al., 2014), with 1852 copies per µm of flagellum length (Daum et al., 2017) (extracted from PDBID: 5O4U).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on P. furiosus flagellar structure.

claim: FlaB0 in Pyrococcus furiosus has 1852 copies per µm of flagellum length.
source: The major filament component in P. furiosus is FlaB0 (Nather et al., 2014), with 1852 copies per µm of flagellum length (Daum et al., 2017) (extracted from PDBID: 5O4U).
evidence: This is data extracted from structural information cited in the manuscript.

claim: FlaB0 is chemically modified with oligosaccharides (35 sugar units per monomer).
source: FlaB0 is chemically modified with oligosaccharides (35 sugar units per monomer) (Daum et al., 2017; Fujinami et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on P. furiosus flagellar modifications.

claim: A large fraction (0.98) of the Pyrococcus furiosus flagellum cost is in the filament.
source: As in E. coli, a large fraction of this cost is in the filament, 0.98.
evidence: This is a calculated value from the detailed cost breakdown.

claim: The rotation of the archaeal flagellum is driven directly by ATP hydrolysis, with 12 ATP used for each rotation in Halobacterium salinarum.
source: The rotation of the archaeal flagellum is driven directly by ATP hydrolysis, and 12 ATP are used for each rotation in Halobacterium salinarum (Iwata et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to literature on archaeal flagellar energetics.

claim: The rotation rate of Halobacterium salinarum flagellum is about 22 Hz.
source: The rotation rate is about 22 Hz (Iwata et al., 2019), but this may be an underestimate because in this measurement the flagellum was loaded with a 210 nm diameter bead, and in E. coli rotation rates decrease with an increased load (Gabel and Berg, 2003).
evidence: This is data from cited literature with a caveat about potential underestimation.

claim: Pyrococcus furiosus can grow at 100°C.
source: P. furiosus has a peculiar metabolism and can grow at 100°C (Kengen, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to literature on P. furiosus physiology.

claim: The operating cost of the Chlamydomonas flagellum determined experimentally on a naked axoneme is 8.8 × 10^4 ATP s^-1 µm^-1.
source: The operating cost of the Chlamydomonas flagellum determined experimentally on a naked axoneme (flagellum without the membrane) is 8.8 × 104 ATP s–1 µm–1 (Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is data from cited literature on Chlamydomonas flagellar energetics.

claim: The operating cost for a generic eukaryotic flagellum is 6.0 × 10^4 ATP s^-1 µm^-1.
source: This is similar to estimates for a generic eukaryotic flagellum, 6.0 × 104 ATP s–1 µm–1 (Raven and Richardson, 1984); Paramecium caudatum, 5.6 × 104 ATP s–1 µm–1 (Katsu-Kimura et al., 2009) (Methods), assuming a total flagellum length of 1.70 × 105 µm (Figure 1—source data 1); and sea urchin sperm, 6.2 × 104 ATP s–1 µm–1 (Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is data from cited literature on eukaryotic flagellar energetics.

claim: The operating cost for Paramecium caudatum flagellum is 5.6 × 10^4 ATP s^-1 µm^-1.
source: This is similar to estimates for a generic eukaryotic flagellum, 6.0 × 104 ATP s–1 µm–1 (Raven and Richardson, 1984); Paramecium caudatum, 5.6 × 104 ATP s–1 µm–1 (Katsu-Kimura et al., 2009) (Methods), assuming a total flagellum length of 1.70 × 105 µm (Figure 1—source data 1); and sea urchin sperm, 6.2 × 104 ATP s–1 µm–1 (Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is data from cited literature on Paramecium flagellar energetics.

claim: The operating cost for sea urchin sperm flagellum is 6.2 × 10^4 ATP s^-1 µm^-1.
source: This is similar to estimates for a generic eukaryotic flagellum, 6.0 × 104 ATP s–1 µm–1 (Raven and Richardson, 1984); Paramecium caudatum, 5.6 × 104 ATP s–1 µm–1 (Katsu-Kimura et al., 2009) (Methods), assuming a total flagellum length of 1.70 × 105 µm (Figure 1—source data 1); and sea urchin sperm, 6.2 × 104 ATP s–1 µm–1 (Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is data from cited literature on sea urchin sperm flagellar energetics.

claim: Chlamydomonas flagella are 11 µm in length.
source: Combining axoneme, membrane, and IFT, and assuming two flagella of 11 µm in length (Tuxhorn et al., 1998), we obtain a Chlamydomonas flagellar construction cost of 6.15 × 1010 ATP cell–1.
evidence: This is data from cited literature (Tuxhorn et al., 1998).

claim: Chlamydomonas has enough energy in its operating budget to swim continuously.
source: Comparing the flagellar operating cost (6.39 × 1010 ATP) to just the cell operating cost (2.4 × 1011 ATP per cell cycle) reveals that, unlike for E. coli, Chlamydomonas has enough energy in its operating budget to swim continuously.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of calculated operating costs.

claim: The absolute flagellar construction cost for bacteria spans 3.6 orders of magnitude, from 1.2 × 10^8 to 4.4 × 10^11 ATP.
source: The absolute flagellar construction cost for bacteria spans 3.6 orders of magnitude, from 1.2 × 108–4.4 × 1011 ATP (Figure 1A), with a median of 7.3 × 108 ATP.
evidence: This is a summary of the data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The median absolute flagellar construction cost for bacteria is 7.3 × 10^8 ATP.
source: The absolute flagellar construction cost for bacteria spans 3.6 orders of magnitude, from 1.2 × 108–4.4 × 1011 ATP (Figure 1A), with a median of 7.3 × 108 ATP.
evidence: This is a summary statistic calculated from the data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The relative flagellar construction cost for bacteria spans 2.3 orders of magnitude, from 0.43% to 96%.
source: The relative flagellar construction cost spans 2.3 orders of magnitude, from 0.43% to 96% (Figure 1B), with a median of 3.7%.
evidence: This is a summary of the data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The median relative flagellar construction cost for bacteria is 3.7%.
source: The relative flagellar construction cost spans 2.3 orders of magnitude, from 0.43% to 96% (Figure 1B), with a median of 3.7%.
evidence: This is a summary statistic calculated from the data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The absolute cost of bacterial flagella increases with bacterial cell volume.
source: The absolute cost of flagella increases with bacterial cell volume, but there is no discernible pattern relating relative costs and cell volume.
evidence: This is observed in Figure 1A and described in the text.

claim: There is no discernible pattern relating bacterial relative flagellar costs and cell volume.
source: The absolute cost of flagella increases with bacterial cell volume, but there is no discernible pattern relating relative costs and cell volume.
evidence: This is observed in Figure 1B and described in the text.

claim: The absolute flagellar construction cost for eukaryotes spans 5.3 orders of magnitude, from 2.2 × 10^10 to 4.2 × 10^15 ATP.
source: The absolute flagellar construction cost for eukaryotes spans 5.3 orders of magnitude, from 2.2 × 1010–4.2 × 1015 ATP (Figure 1A), with a median of 1.8 × 1011 ATP.
evidence: This is a summary of the data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The median absolute flagellar construction cost for eukaryotes is 1.8 × 10^11 ATP.
source: The absolute flagellar construction cost for eukaryotes spans 5.3 orders of magnitude, from 2.2 × 1010–4.2 × 1015 ATP (Figure 1A), with a median of 1.8 × 1011 ATP.
evidence: This is a summary statistic calculated from the data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The relative flagellar construction cost for eukaryotes spans 3.1 orders of magnitude, from 0.037% to 44%.
source: The relative flagellar construction cost spans 3.1 orders of magnitude, from 0.037% to 44% (Figure 1B), with a median of 3.0%.
evidence: This is a summary of the data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The median relative flagellar construction cost for eukaryotes is 3.0%.
source: The relative flagellar construction cost spans 3.1 orders of magnitude, from 0.037% to 44% (Figure 1B), with a median of 3.0%.
evidence: This is a summary statistic calculated from the data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Eukaryotic flagellates have lower absolute flagellum costs than the hyperflagellated ciliates and parabasalids, even where cell volumes overlap.
source: Eukaryotic flagellates (euglenids, kinetoplastids, and other eukaryotes), carrying a small number of flagella, have lower absolute flagellum costs than the hyperflagellated ciliates and parabasalids. This is true even where cell volumes overlap.
evidence: This is observed in Figure 1A and described in the text.

claim: A power law fit to the eukaryotic flagellate absolute cost data has an exponent of 0.31±0.03.
source: A power law fit to the eukaryotic flagellate absolute cost data has an exponent of 0.31±0.03, and a joint fit to the ciliates and parabasalids has an exponent of 0.86±0.10.
evidence: This is a statistical fit to the data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: A joint power law fit to the ciliates and parabasalids absolute cost data has an exponent of 0.86±0.10.
source: A power law fit to the eukaryotic flagellate absolute cost data has an exponent of 0.31±0.03, and a joint fit to the ciliates and parabasalids has an exponent of 0.86±0.10.
evidence: This is a statistical fit to the data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Eukaryotic flagellates follow a power law scaling of relative construction cost with cell volume with an exponent of -0.66±0.03.
source: Here, the eukaryotic flagellates follow a power law scaling with an exponent of –0.66±0.03.
evidence: This is a statistical fit to the data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Swimming speed increases weakly with cell volume when all species are examined together (power law exponent = 0.13±0.03).
source: Swimming speeds were obtained from the literature for a subset of species from our cost dataset, revealing that swimming speed increases weakly with cell volume when all species are examined together (power law exponent ± SE = 0.13±0.03) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a statistical fit to the data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: For eukaryotic flagellates, swimming speed is volume-independent (exponent = 0.02 ± 0.09).
source: When focussing on just eukaryotic flagellates, we find a volume-independent swimming speed (examined in more detail in the next section), exponent = 0.02 ± 0.09 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a statistical fit to the data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Swimming speed increases with absolute flagellar construction cost (exponent = 0.16 ± 0.03).
source: Besides increasing with cell volume, the swimming speed also increases with absolute flagellar construction cost (exponent = 0.16 ± 0.03; Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a statistical fit to the data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Bacterial and eukaryotic flagella follow a common trend in their ability to generate swimming speed per ATP invested.
source: To allow for a direct comparison between the two groups, swimming speed is expressed in cell lengths per second per ATP invested, revealing that bacterial and eukaryotic flagella follow a common trend (Figure 2C), suggesting that there is no large difference in cost-effectiveness between the two groups once scaling with cell size has been taken into consideration.
evidence: This is observed in Figure 2C and described in the text.

claim: There is no large difference in cost-effectiveness between bacterial and eukaryotic flagella once scaling with cell size has been taken into consideration.
source: To allow for a direct comparison between the two groups, swimming speed is expressed in cell lengths per second per ATP invested, revealing that bacterial and eukaryotic flagella follow a common trend (Figure 2C), suggesting that there is no large difference in cost-effectiveness between the two groups once scaling with cell size has been taken into consideration.
evidence: This is inferred from the common trend observed in Figure 2C.

claim: Eukaryotes have a mean efficiency of 0.7% for the conversion of chemical energy (ATP) into swimming power.
source: Comparing these two operating costs (Figure 2D) reveals that eukaryotes have a mean efficiency of 0.7% for the conversion of chemical energy (ATP) into swimming power, which is similar to earlier reports of swimming efficiencies for single-celled organisms (Chattopadhyay et al., 2006; Osterman and Vilfan, 2011; Purcell, 1997).
evidence: This is calculated from the comparison shown in Figure 2D and is consistent with cited literature.

claim: For species with a cell volume <10^2 µm^3, flagella constitute a net loss in nutrients and decrease in growth rate in a homogenous medium.
source: For species with a cell volume <102 µm3, flagella constitute a net loss in nutrients and decrease in growth rate (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is calculated using the relative growth rate equation and shown in Figure 2E.

claim: For species with a cell volume >10^3 µm^3, flagella can provide a net gain in nutrients and constitute an increase in growth rate.
source: For species with a cell volume >103 µm3, flagella can provide a net gain in nutrients and therefore constitute an increase in growth rate.
evidence: This is calculated using the relative growth rate equation and shown in Figure 2E.

claim: For small cell volumes (<10^2 µm^3), flagella cannot profitably be used for gathering nutrients in a homogenous medium.
source: This suggest that for these species, flagella cannot profitably be used for gathering nutrients in a homogenous medium.
evidence: This is inferred from the negative relative growth rate for small cells shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The empirically determined exponent for the relation between cell volume and relative flagellar construction cost in eukaryotic flagellates (-0.66±0.03) matches the theoretically derived exponent (-0.64±0.04).
source: The exponent in Equation 6 matches with the empirically determined exponent for eukaryotic flagellates (which excludes ciliates and parabasalids), –0.66±0.03 (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a comparison between the theoretical model and empirical data.

claim: The scaling of flagellar construction cost in eukaryotic flagellates is determined by simple physical principles combined with the fact that swimming speeds do not vary with cell volume.
source: This suggests that the scaling of flagellar construction cost is determined by simple physical principles combined with the fact that swimming speeds do not vary with cell volume.
evidence: This is inferred from the match between theoretical and empirical scaling relationships.

claim: There appears to be a soft lower limit to the swimming speed of eukaryotic flagellates.
source: Another corollary of this result is that there appears to be a (soft) lower limit to the swimming speed of eukaryotic flagellates, as there is a distinct lack of eukaryotic species in the grey shaded triangular area shown in Figure 1B.
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of data points in a specific region of Figure 1B.

claim: Low copy number flagellar proteins are expected to be more variable in length than those in high copy number, especially in species with small effective population sizes.
source: The key point is that low copy number flagellar proteins are expected to be more variable in length than those in high copy number, especially in species with small effective population sizes.
evidence: This is inferred from the analysis of relative costs of amino acid additions shown in Figure 3.

claim: The cheapest eukaryotic flagella are more expensive than the entire cells of many bacterial species.
source: To answer this question, we first compare the absolute construction cost of entire bacterial cells to the construction cost of eukaryotic flagella (Figure 4A), revealing that the cheapest eukaryotic flagella are in fact more expensive than the entire cells of many bacterial species.
evidence: This is observed in Figure 4A and described in the text.

claim: Most bacterial species cannot afford full length eukaryotic flagella.
source: Next, we examine the observed absolute flagellar investment in these bacterial species and ask what length of eukaryotic flagellum they could afford. These lengths are compared with the total flagellum length of eukaryotic species, revealing that most bacterial species cannot afford full length eukaryotic flagella (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is observed in Figure 4B and described in the text.

claim: All eukaryotic flagella that have been observed appear to be long and slender.
source: Two observations suggest that the short and stumpy eukaryotic flagella these bacteria could afford would be highly ineffective. First, all eukaryotic flagella that have been observed, appear to be long and slender.
evidence: This is based on general observations of eukaryotic flagellar morphology.

claim: All small eukaryotes have a high relative investment in flagella.
source: Second, all small eukaryotes have a high relative investment in flagella (Figure 1B), suggesting that short (but cheaper) flagella are not up to the task.
evidence: This is observed in Figure 1B and described in the text.

claim: Reducing the cost of the eukaryotic flagellum by decreasing the number of microtubule doublets occurs in some species but its rarity suggests that it is associated with a considerable reduction in swimming ability.
source: Reducing the cost of the eukaryotic flagellum by decreasing the number of microtubule doublets occurs in some species (Prensier et al., 1980; Schrevel and Besse, 1975), but its rarity suggests that it is associated with a considerable reduction in swimming ability.
evidence: This is inferred from the rarity of reduced microtubule doublet structures in nature, with citations to examples.

claim: The basic machinery that operates the eukaryotic flagellum may have evolved in a small prokaryote-sized cell, but the common eukaryotic flagellum with this machinery present all along its length could only evolve in larger cells.
source: Thus, the basic machinery that operates the eukaryotic flagellum, for example, outer doublet microtubules, dynein motors, and radial spokes, may have evolved in a small prokaryote-sized cell; but the common eukaryotic flagellum, with this machinery present all along its length, could only evolve in larger cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the analysis of Micromonas pusilla and the cost constraints on small cells.

claim: Micromonas pusilla has a cell volume of about 1 µm^3 and a eukaryotic flagellum.
source: Consider the small alga Micromonas pusilla which has a cell volume of about 1 µm3 and a eukaryotic flagellum (Simon et al., 2017).
evidence: This is data from cited literature on Micromonas pusilla.

claim: In Micromonas pusilla, the outer microtubule doublets and motor proteins are only present in the proximal 10-20% of the flagellar length.
source: Here, however, unlike most eukaryotic flagella, the outer microtubule doublets and motor proteins are only present in the proximal 10–20% of the flagellar length. The remainder of the flagellum consists of the inner pair microtubules surrounded by a membrane (Vaulot et al., 2008).
evidence: This is data from cited literature on Micromonas pusilla flagellar structure.

claim: There appears to be a minimum swimming speed for eukaryotic flagellates, independent of cell volume.
source: There appears to be a minimum swimming speed for eukaryotic flagellates, independent of cell volume.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of swimming speed data in Figure 2A.

claim: Flagella in small cells cannot be maintained solely for the collection of nutrients in homogenous media.
source: Flagella in small cells cannot be maintained solely for the collection of nutrients in homogenous media.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the relative growth rate analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Proteins from the same flagella but with lower copy numbers may experience a more permissive evolutionary environment, being able to accumulate amino acids neutrally and requiring lower beneficial effects for amino acid additions to be favoured by selection.
